title: Notation
summary: VIO state, coordinate frames, and rigid-body coordinate transformations.

content.text: Visual–inertial odometry (VIO) combines camera and inertial measurements to estimate the metric six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) motion of a sensing platform: three-dimensional position and orientation. Images constrain motion through observations of the surrounding scene, while IMU measurements constrain motion between image timestamps.

We describe the platform motion using three coordinate frames: the global frame \(\{G\}\), the IMU frame \(\{I\}\), and the camera frame \(\{C\}\). The global frame provides the coordinates in which we express the estimated trajectory; the IMU and camera frames move with their respective sensors.

content.alt: Global frame G, rigidly mounted IMU frame I and camera frame C, and a fixed environment point f. A blue connector denotes the IMU pose; dotted lines indicate point positions and visual observation.
content.caption: Global, IMU, and camera frames. The camera and IMU form a rigid sensor platform. The blue connector denotes a pose relation, not a trajectory. Dotted lines relate the same environment point \(f\) to the frames.

Here, \({}^{G}\mathbf{p}_{I}\) and \({}^{G}\mathbf{v}_{I}\) are the IMU position and velocity expressed in the global frame. The rotation matrix \({}^{I}_{G}\mathbf{R}\) maps vector coordinates from the global frame into the IMU frame. The vectors \(\mathbf{b}_{g}\) and \(\mathbf{b}_{a}\) are the gyroscope and accelerometer biases. Velocity and biases are estimated alongside pose because they affect the integration of inertial measurements.

The frame labels specify how each quantity should be read. For a position, the superscript identifies the frame in which its coordinates are expressed, and the subscript identifies the object. Thus, \({}^{G}\mathbf{p}_{I}\) is the position of the IMU origin expressed in \(\{G\}\). For a rotation, the lower frame label is the source and the upper label is the destination.

Subtracting the IMU position first expresses the point relative to the IMU origin; the rotation then expresses that displacement along the IMU axes.

A rigid-body coordinate transformation combines rotation and translation in one matrix. We write \({}^{A}_{B}\mathbf{T}\) for the transform that maps point coordinates from frame \(\{B\}\) into frame \(\{A\}\). Appending a 1 to a three-dimensional point gives its homogeneous coordinates. These operations change how the same point is expressed in different frames.

The camera–IMU extrinsic transform \({}^{C}_{I}\mathbf{T}\) maps IMU coordinates into camera coordinates. Its rotation block is \({}^{C}_{I}\mathbf{R}\), and its translation block is the IMU origin expressed in \(\{C\}\). For rigidly mounted sensors, this transform is constant. title: Camera and IMU measurement models
summary: Image projection, gyroscope angular rate, and accelerometer specific force.

content.text: A camera records an array of pixel intensities or colors at each image timestamp. Feature detection and tracking extract two-dimensional point coordinates from these images. A projection model relates those coordinates to the three-dimensional geometry viewed by the camera. We use point coordinates as a representative observation; direct methods can instead compare image intensities.

Let \({}^{C}\mathbf{p}_f=(X,Y,Z)^\top\) denote an environment point expressed in the camera frame. We take the camera's optical axis as \(+Z_C\), with \(X_C\) pointing right and \(Y_C\) down in the image. For an ideal pinhole camera with known intrinsics, zero skew, and no lens distortion, its observed pixel coordinates \(\mathbf{z}_f=(u,v)^\top\) follow:

The focal lengths \(f_x,f_y\) and principal-point coordinates \(c_x,c_y\) are expressed in pixels. The principal point is where the optical axis meets the ideal image plane. The point coordinates \(X,Y,Z\) use a common length unit; in VIO we express them in meters. Here \(Z\) is depth along the optical axis. The term \(\mathbf{n}_c\) represents error in the extracted pixel coordinates, not noise in pixel intensity. This example assumes ideal or undistorted observations.

content.caption: One image coordinate, multiple possible depths. The hollow points \({}^{C}\mathbf{p}_f\) and \(\lambda\,{}^{C}\mathbf{p}_f\), with \(\lambda>1\), are alternative positions consistent with the same ideal observation \(\mathbf{z}_f\). The virtual image plane is drawn in front of the camera center. Measurement noise is omitted in this schematic \(\left(\mathbf{n}_c=\mathbf{0}\right)\).

The camera pose determines a fixed environment point's coordinates in \(\{C\}\) and therefore its predicted projection. Observations of fixed points across images provide constraints on camera motion and scene geometry. The transform between camera and IMU coordinates is described in

An IMU provides timestamped, three-axis gyroscope and accelerometer readings, rather than direct orientation, velocity, or position measurements. We use an additive model with scale and axis errors assumed corrected or negligible. Readings are expressed along the common IMU axes. We neglect Earth rotation, treat \(\{G\}\) as locally inertial, and assume constant gravity.
The gyroscope measures angular velocity, which describes how orientation changes over time. Its measurement model is

Here \({}^{I}\boldsymbol{\omega}\) is the IMU's angular velocity relative to \(\{G\}\), expressed along the IMU axes. Its direction gives the instantaneous rotation axis under the right-hand rule, and its magnitude gives angular speed; neither specifies the current orientation. The vectors \(\mathbf{b}_g\) and \(\mathbf{n}_g\) are bias and measurement noise. All terms have units of radians per second. For the global-to-IMU rotation \({}^{I}_{G}\mathbf{R}\),

A dot denotes a time derivative, and \([\mathbf{u}]_{\times}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\) defines the cross-product matrix. The minus sign follows the global-to-IMU coordinate convention. Integration requires an initial orientation relative to the chosen \(\{G\}\); the gyroscope does not supply it. Integrating the three components independently does not generally give roll, pitch, and yaw.

Bias and noise play different roles. We model bias as an unknown offset that may change slowly, and noise as zero-mean random measurement error. An estimator subtracts an estimated bias before integration; the true bias and individual noise samples remain unknown. Bias errors and noise both affect the integrated state. Zero-mean noise need not cancel over a finite interval.
The accelerometer measures specific force, the non-gravitational force per unit mass acting on the sensor. Its measurement model is

Here \({}^{G}\mathbf{a}_I=d({}^{G}\mathbf{v}_I)/dt\) is the IMU origin's motion acceleration and \({}^{G}\mathbf{g}\) is gravitational acceleration, both expressed in \(\{G\}\). The reading \(\mathbf{a}_m\), bias \(\mathbf{b}_a\), and noise \(\mathbf{n}_a\) use IMU axes and have units of meters per second squared, as do the global acceleration terms. The same bias/noise distinction applies to both sensors.

Rotating the bias-corrected reading into \(\{G\}\) with \(({}^{I}_{G}\mathbf{R})^\top\) and adding gravity gives an acceleration estimate. An incorrect tilt can produce apparent motion acceleration even at rest. Velocity and position then require time integration and their initial values.

For a stationary, bias-free, noiseless sensor with aligned global and IMU axes and \(+z\) upward, \({}^{G}\mathbf{a}_I=\mathbf{0}\) and \({}^{G}\mathbf{g}=(0,0,-g)^\top\), with \(g>0\). Its accelerometer reads \((0,0,g)^\top\): the table supports it against gravity. In ideal, non-rotating free fall it reads zero, even though the sensor accelerates under gravity.
